lead: A wireless sensor network (WSN) is a group of small battery-powered nodes. Each senses the world, processes the reading, and passes it hop by hop to one collector called the sink. No node needs a cable or long radio range. WSNs suit crop fields, pipelines, factory machines, forest-fire watch and bridge strain. This chapter gives the elements, topologies, protocol layers, energy arithmetic and open challenges.
prereq: You need 2.3 for the five parts of a sensor node and 2.5 for the microcontroller that runs the stack.

blocks.text: A WSN has three elements. A sensor node is a smart object (see 2.3) with a sensing unit, processing unit, radio transceiver and power unit. A sink, or base station, collects data from the field and usually has mains power. A gateway links the sink to the outside world, for example over 4G.

Nodes differ from ordinary computers in three ways: they run on a battery or harvester, so energy is the first constraint; their radio is short range; and they are many—hundreds or thousands. The network moves a few bytes a long distance, not many bytes a short distance.

Three topologies cover most designs. In a star every node talks directly to the sink: simple, one hop, but the sink must be in range of every node. In a tree each node sends to a parent that forwards upward; reach grows, but a dead parent cuts off its children. In a mesh any node may forward for any neighbour, giving many paths and fault tolerance at the cost of more routing work.
A path with more than one hop is multi-hop, the normal case, because radio energy grows with distance.

sections.h3: The stack and the listening problem

blocks.text: A node runs a small stack. The physical layer turns bits into modulation and sets transmit power. The MAC layer decides when a node may use the shared channel. The routing layer picks the next hop towards the sink. The transport layer keeps end-to-end reliability where needed. The application layer runs the sensing task and aggregation.

The radio is the biggest energy consumer. A node spends energy transmitting, receiving, and—worst—listening for a packet that may never arrive. Idle listening can draw nearly as much power as receiving. So the MAC layer uses duty cycling: the radio sleeps most of the time and wakes on a schedule.

A contention-based MAC lets a node transmit when it has data and back off after a collision; simple and adaptive, but collisions waste energy. A schedule-based MAC gives each node a fixed slot; no collisions, but slots are wasted when a node has nothing to send. Most designs mix both.
A sleeping node cannot hear. Sender and receiver must share wake times, so the MAC also handles time synchronisation and the cost of a long preamble that holds the receiver awake.

Three routing ideas appear in every course. Flooding: each node rebroadcasts every packet once; it finds a path if one exists, but wastes energy on duplicates. Gossiping: a node forwards to one random neighbour, which cuts duplicates but may never deliver. LEACH: nodes form clusters, each elects a head that aggregates readings into one packet for the sink, and the head role rotates so no single node drains first.

Directed diffusion is data-centric: the sink broadcasts an interest, matching nodes send data back along the path the interest came from, and the sink reinforces the best path. Only a few universities examine it; remember the idea—name the data, not the node.
E_tx(k, d) = k × E_elec + k × ε × d²
blocks.where: E_tx is transmit energy in joules; k is bits; E_elec is electronics energy per bit, typically 50 nJ/bit; ε is amplifier energy per bit per square metre (100 pJ/bit/m² in this book's examples); d is distance in metres. Receiving k bits costs k × E_elec.

blocks.text: Splitting d into n equal hops changes the amplifier cost from εd² to n × ε(d/n)² = εd²/n, but the electronics cost becomes n × E_elec. So transmit energy per bit is n × E_elec + εd²/n: only the amplifier part falls, by the factor n.

items: Coverage: every point of the field lies within sensing range of at least one node.
Connectivity: every node has a path to the sink, and above a density threshold it holds almost surely.
Localisation: each node finds its own position, from GPS, anchor nodes, or ranging.
Time synchronisation: nodes agree on a clock so wake schedules and timestamps line up; drift makes this a repeating task.

blocks.text: Network lifetime has at least three definitions: time until the first node dies, time until a stated fraction die, and time until coverage or connectivity breaks so the network stops delivering usable data. The first is strictest and commonest in exams. The challenges follow: limited energy, changing topology as nodes die, fault tolerance, clock drift and security.

figure.caption: One hop follows the curve: 100 m costs 1050 nJ/bit and 200 m costs 4050. The lower points split the same distances into 50 m hops: 600 nJ/bit at 100 m and 1200 nJ/bit at 200 m, saving 450 (42.9%) and 2850 (70.4%).

spec.aria: A plot of energy per bit against total distance: the one-hop curve passes through 1050 nJ/bit at 100 m and 4050 at 200 m, while points for 50 m hops lie below at 600 and 1200 nJ/bit.

examples.question: A sensor node must send data to a sink 100 m away. The radio uses E_elec = 50 nJ/bit and ε = 100 pJ/bit/m². Compare the energy per bit for a direct 100 m hop with a two-hop path of 50 m per hop. Give the saving in nJ per bit and as a percentage.
steps: Model: E = E_elec + εd² joules per bit, with d in metres.
Use E_elec = 50 nJ/bit and ε = 100 × 10⁻¹² J/bit/m².
Direct 100 m: εd² = 1000 nJ; total = 50 + 1000 = 1050 nJ/bit.
One 50 m hop: εd² = 250 nJ; total = 50 + 250 = 300 nJ/bit.
examples.answer: Two 50 m hops cost 600 nJ per bit against 1050 nJ for one 100 m hop, a saving of 450 nJ per bit, about 42.9 %.
examples.check:
E_elec = 50e-9
eps = 100e-12
d_direct = 100.0
d_hop = 50.0
E_direct = (E_elec + eps * d_direct**2) * 1e9
E_hop = (E_elec + eps * d_hop**2) * 1e9
E_two = 2 * E_hop
saving = E_direct - E_two
pct = saving / E_direct * 100
print(round(E_direct, 2))
print(round(E_two, 2))
print(round(saving, 2))
print(round(pct, 2))

examples.question: For the same radio, how much does one hop of 200 m cost per bit, and how does it compare with four hops of 50 m? Ignore receive energy unless told otherwise.
steps: Direct 200 m: εd² = 4000 nJ; total = 50 + 4000 = 4050 nJ/bit.
examples.answer: The direct 200 m hop costs 4050 nJ per bit and four 50 m hops cost 1200 nJ per bit, a saving of 2850 nJ per bit, about 70.4 %.

traps: A WSN is not Wi-Fi. Nodes are battery-limited and multi-hop; no access point reaches every node in one hop.
Multi-hop is not free. It saves transmit energy but adds latency, routing overhead and a receive cost at every relay; at high hop counts total energy can rise.

Unit slips in the radio model: ε is in pJ (10⁻¹² J), not nJ, and d is squared in metres. Using 100 in place of 100 × 10⁻¹² inflates the amplifier term by 10¹²; writing 100 nJ/bit/m² where 100 pJ/bit/m² is meant inflates it by 10³. Check the prefix before squaring d.
Sink, gateway and node are different. The node senses, the sink collects, the gateway leaves the network.
Flooding and gossiping are not table-driven routing protocols. Flooding guarantees delivery and wastes energy; gossiping saves energy and may never deliver.

quiz.q: Define a wireless sensor network and name its three elements.
quiz.a: A WSN is a set of small sensor nodes that sense, process and forward data hop by hop to a sink. Elements: sensor nodes, the sink or base station, and the gateway.
Keeping the radio asleep most of the time and waking it on a schedule, so idle-listening energy is cut.

quiz.q: Why is idle listening called the enemy of a WSN?
quiz.a: A listening radio draws almost as much power as a receiving one, and a node may listen for hours with no packet. Idle listening can dominate the energy budget, so duty cycling is used.

quiz.q: With E_elec = 50 nJ/bit and ε = 100 pJ/bit/m², find the energy per bit for a 200 m direct hop and for four hops of 50 m.
quiz.a: Amplifier term = 100 × 10⁻¹² × 40 000 = 4000 nJ/bit. Total = 50 + 4000 = 4050 nJ/bit. Each 50 m hop: 50 + 250 = 300 nJ/bit, four hops = 1200 nJ/bit. Saving = 2850 nJ/bit, about 70.4 %.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a star topology against a mesh.
quiz.a: Star: simple, one hop, little routing overhead, but the sink must reach every node, so a distant node is lost. Mesh: many paths and fault tolerance, but more routing overhead and more receive energy at relays.

quiz.q: Why does LEACH rotate the cluster-head role?
quiz.a: A permanent head spends far more energy than its members, on aggregation and long-range transmission. Rotating spreads that cost across nodes, so the first node dies later and network lifetime rises.

quiz.q: Two reports give network lifetimes of 40 days and 90 days for the same deployment. How can both be right?
quiz.a: Lifetime is defined differently. 40 days is the time until the first node dies; 90 days is the time until a stated fraction die, or until coverage or connectivity breaks. Always ask which definition is used.

quiz.q: What is localisation and why does a WSN need it?
quiz.a: Localisation is a node finding its own position, from GPS, anchor nodes or ranging. A reading such as 34 °C is useless unless you know where it was taken.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial WSN work now runs on time-slotted channel hopping, where nodes share a repeating slot frame instead of contending, making latency predictable and saving energy. Energy-harvesting nodes that run for years without a battery change are a live research area. Machine learning on the node compresses data before transmission, because a byte never sent costs nothing. Search for 'TSCH', '6TiSCH', 'energy harvesting WSN' and 'sink mobility' to go further.
